title: Stanford's Tutor CoPilot, which runs on GPT-4, helps tutors raise students' topic mastery by 4 percentage points in a randomized trial with 900 tutors; end-of-year math scores show no significant gain
summary: Tutor CoPilot, a Stanford system built on GPT-4 that suggests moves to human tutors, made students 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, with no significant gain on end-of-year tests.
account: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb and Demszky of Stanford built Tutor CoPilot, a language-model system that gives human tutors expert-like suggestions during live sessions. They tested it with FEV Tutor, a virtual tutoring provider, and a large southern U.S. school district serving over 30,000 students. Nine schools took part. The district identified 1,787 students in grades 3–8, 80% Hispanic, who had performed below grade level. The preprint (arXiv, 3 October 2024) says that the study started at the end of March 2024 and lasted two months. Version 3 of the preprint (10 October 2026) dates the trial from 27 March to 17 May 2024. The 900 tutors were evenly split between treatment and control. Students of treated tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics. Students of lower-rated tutors gained 9 points. The authors put the cost at about $20 per tutor per year. The 74 (7 October 2024) and MIT Technology Review (28 October 2024) reported that the system runs on OpenAI's GPT-4. They gave pass rates of 66% versus 62% on exit assessments and quoted outside researchers' caveats about the basic level of the mathematics. Education Week (31 October 2024), quoting co-author Susanna Loeb, reported that tutors using the tool were more likely to prompt students to explain. They were less likely to give away solutions. The 74 reported on 29 January 2025 that FEV Tutor, the provider that ran the trial, had shut down on 25 January 2025 after failing to raise money or find a buyer. In version 3 of the preprint, the authors report that they found no significant gain on end-of-year math tests.
purpose: Tutor CoPilot was built to scale expert tutoring guidance to novice tutors in real time. Higher student mastery is that purpose.
system: Tutor CoPilot using GPT-4 and Bridge teaching strategies within FEV Tutor’s platform
developer: Stanford University (Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky)
deployer: FEV Tutor with a large southern U.S. school district (nine schools)

ratings.reason: Students of tutors with the tool were 4 percentage points more likely to pass session exit tickets (62% to 66%), and 9 points for lower-rated tutors. The authors found no significant gain on end-of-year tests.
The provider's tutors with the tool prompted students to explain more often and gave generic praise less often, at about $20 per tutor per year.

ai_role.statement: Tutors were randomized to have access to the tool or not, so the 4-point gain measures the effect of access. Among sessions where tutors used it, the authors estimate a 14-point gain. The model suggested moves to the human tutor, and the tutor chose what to say to the student.

fields.summary: Tutor CoPilot, a Stanford system built on GPT-4 that suggests moves to human tutors, made students 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, with no significant gain on end-of-year tests.
fields.account: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb and Demszky of Stanford built Tutor CoPilot, a language-model system that gives human tutors expert-like suggestions during live sessions. They tested it with FEV Tutor, a virtual tutoring provider, and a large southern U.S. school district serving over 30,000 students. Nine schools took part. The district identified 1,787 students in grades 3–8, 80% Hispanic, who had performed below grade level. The preprint (arXiv, 3 October 2024) says that the study started at the end of March 2024 and lasted two months. Version 3 of the preprint (10 October 2026) dates the trial from 27 March to 17 May 2024. The 900 tutors were evenly split between treatment and control. Students of treated tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics. Students of lower-rated tutors gained 9 points. The authors put the cost at about $20 per tutor per year. The 74 (7 October 2024) and MIT Technology Review (28 October 2024) reported that the system runs on OpenAI's GPT-4. They gave pass rates of 66% versus 62% on exit assessments and quoted outside researchers' caveats about the basic level of the mathematics. Education Week (31 October 2024), quoting co-author Susanna Loeb, reported that tutors using the tool were more likely to prompt students to explain. They were less likely to give away solutions. The 74 reported on 29 January 2025 that FEV Tutor, the provider that ran the trial, had shut down on 25 January 2025 after failing to raise money or find a buyer. In version 3 of the preprint, the authors report that they found no significant gain on end-of-year math tests.
